proxy_language: Proto-Yeniseian (with Ket as primary attested model; Kott/Assan/Arin/Pumpokol data as secondary)
proxy_rationale: Afontova Gora (c. 20-12 ka) and Kokorevo (c. 14-10 ka) are Upper Palaeolithic sites on the Yenisei near Krasnoyarsk. No language can be tied to them; the 12-20 ka gap to any attested language is far beyond the reach of the comparative method. Yeniseian is the only language family historically rooted in the Upper/Middle Yenisei basin and is a language isolate-like family with deep time depth, so it is the least arbitrary proxy for a Siberian Palaeolithic name set. This is a convention for the game, not a claim of continuity; Yeniseian speakers probably arrived from the south (Baikal/Sayan area) much later. Proto-Yeniseian forms follow Starostin, Vajda and Werner reconstructions and are marked as reconstructed.
phonology: Ket consonants: stops /p t k q/ with /b d g/ (voiced series marginal in some positions), /ʔ/ glottal stop; affricates /ts tʃ/; fricatives /s x/ (and /h/), /ɣ/ in some analyses; nasals /m n ŋ/; liquids /l/ (rare in native words), /r/ marginal; glides /j w/. Ket uvular /q/ is phonemic and contrasts with /k/. Vowels: /i e a o u/ plus mid/central /ɨ ə/ in some analyses; length contrast; Ket has four tones (Vajda) with a tonal/glottalization system largely in the 'laryngealized' vs. plain contrast. Proto-Yeniseian reconstruction (Starostin 1982, Vajda/Werner 2020) posits a larger consonant system with a 3-way stop contrast reduced in daughters, plus a glottalized/pharyngealized series and tone-bearing syllables.
phonotactics: Roots are mostly monosyllabic or disyllabic: CV, CVC, CVV, CVCV, CVCVC; (C)V(C) is the core. Initial consonant clusters are rare to absent in native roots; word-initial vowels are uncommon (a glottal onset is often present). Final consonants: mainly /n ŋ k q s t l m j/. Medial clusters allowed with sonorant or nasal first (-nk-, -ŋk-, -lt-, -st-). Voiced stops and /b/ occur mostly after nasals or in loans. No long sequences of vowels beyond VV; vowel harmony absent. Names should favor 1-3 syllables.
orthography: Use a simplified Latinised scholarly transliteration of Ket/Yeniseian: p t k q b d g s x h ts ch (for tʃ) m n ng (for ŋ) l r j w y; vowels a e i o u plus long vowels written doubled (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu); glottal stop as an apostrophe ' (no tone marks). Avoid diacritics except the optional macron-free doubling. Proto-Yeniseian reconstructions are written with an asterisk (e.g. *qo-).
morphology: Yeniseian is polysynthetic with highly complex verbal morphology (position-class template with 20+ slots, discontinuous agreement) and relatively simple nouns. Nouns: no case in the strict sense but a system of postpositions/clitics (-ŋa, -ga, -di, -da, -sa for locative/dative/etc.), gender classes (masculine, feminine, inanimate for animals/humans/things; Ket has 3 classes), plural in -ŋ/-n/-in/-an (e.g. -ŋ, -nan) and class-based plural. Noun roots are typically monosyllabic with one or two derivational suffixes. Possession is expressed by prefixing a personal prefix (ku- 'my', di- 'thy' etc.). Yeniseian is notable for body-part and kinship terms with inalienable prefixes.
compounding: Compounding is productive: noun-noun compounds are head-final (modifier + head), e.g. Ket 'water-hole' type formations. Genitive constructions use a juxtaposed possessor + possessed with a possessive/genitive suffix -ŋa/-di or simple juxtaposition; 'X of Y' = Y-GEN X or Y X. Agent nouns ('Y-maker') are formed from verb roots with a nominalizing suffix (-ŋ, -s, -tn, -lʔ) or by compounding with a head noun 'person/man' (Ket diŋ 'person, man'). Derived names may add diminutive -'a or augmentative -ŋ.
noun_phrase_order: Modifier before head: adjective/possessor/numeral precedes the noun (e.g. [qʌ̃ʔ] 'big' + noun). Postpositions rather than prepositions. Head-final throughout.

attested_roots.gloss: mammoth (loan from Nenets in Ket tradition)

worked_examples.name: Qoj Dang
worked_examples.gloss: qoj 'reindeer' + dʌ̃ŋ 'man' (Y-agent compound with 'man' as head)

notes: Strictly speaking no linguistic evidence ties the Afontova Gora/Kokorevo cultures to Yeniseian or any attested language; confidence is speculative. Some roots above are modern Ket or Proto-Yeniseian forms chosen as models for naming conventions only; glosses should be treated as approximate, and 'tuk' is a flagged loan in Ket tradition. Names should stay short (1-3 syllables), head-final, with q/k contrast, ng, and sibilants as flavour. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word, since Yeniseian is not Goidelic.
